title: Effectiveness of irrigation systems for removing intracanal medication isthmuses in 3D-printed molars replicas
abstract: Abstract This study evaluated the effectiveness of four irrigation techniques used during root canal treatment [conventional irrigation (CU), Irriflex (IF), Easy Clean (EC), and passive ultrasonic irrigation (PUI)] in removing calcium hydroxide–based and calcium silicate–based intracanal medications from the isthmus of mesial root canals in 3D-printed mandibular molar replicas. A mandibular molar with presence of an isthmus in the mesial roots and moderate curvature was instrumented with Reciproc R40.06, scanned by Micro Computed Tomography (micro-CT), and used as model to create 64 standardized translucent resin replicas. The mesial roots and isthmus areas were filled with Ultracal XS or Bio-C Temp and scanned again. After 7 days, replicas were reinstrumented and subjected to the irrigation protocols, followed by micro-CT analysis of medication removal. The percentage of remaining intracanal medication volume was analyzed using a t-test. The percentage of medication removed in the isthmus area was also calculated and analyzed using two-way ANOVA ( p  < 0.05) to evaluate the effects of different factors, followed by Tukey’s post hoc test for multiple comparisons. PUI promoted the highest removal of Ultracal XS in percentage (98.2 ± 2.28) ( p  < 0.05), with no differences among the other techniques. For Bio-C Temp, all protocols performed similarly. PUI showed similar performance for both medications, while the other techniques removed Bio-C Temp more effectively than Ultracal XS.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The success of root canal treatment depends largely on the effective elimination of bacterial biofilm from the root canal system. This goal, however, can be compromised by anatomical irregularities, such as lateral canals, isthmuses, and apical deltas, which may remain inaccessible to endodontic instruments [ 1 ]. Irrigation therefore plays a critical role in chemomechanical preparation, as irrigating solutions enable the cleaning of areas not reached by instrumentation [ 2 ], contribute to smear layer removal [ 3 ], eliminate hard tissue debris generated by mechanical preparation [ 4 ], and help to reduce bacteria, toxins, and organic residues, all of which are essential to preventing or treating periapical disease [ 5 ].

Among the most complex anatomical challenges is the mesial root of mandibular molars, where isthmuses are highly prevalent [ 5 ,  6 ]. An isthmus, defined as a narrow, ribbon-shaped communication between two canals containing pulp or pulp-derived tissue [ 7 ], occurs frequently in mandibular molars, maxillary premolars, and molars with C-shaped or two-canal roots. The incidence of isthmuses in the mesial root of mandibular first molars is particularly high, up to 81% in the 4–6 mm apical region of individuals aged 20–39 years; however, it decreases significantly with age [ 8 ].

Fan et al. (2010) proposed a classification for isthmus configurations, ranging from wide fusion sheets connecting the mesiobuccal (MB) and mesiolingual (ML) canals (Type I) to tubular communications (Type IV), while some roots show no connection (Type II) [ 9 ]. The variability in these forms is thought to result from differences in dentin fusion, deposition, and calcification during tooth development [ 9 ].

The clinical significance of the isthmus lies in its frequent inaccessibility to instruments, irrigants, and medications, enabling it to act as a reservoir for tissue and bacteria that may compromise nonsurgical root canal treatment [ 10 ]. Studies have shown that gram-positive and gram-negative microorganisms can persist for over a decade in the nutrient-deficient environment of an isthmus, even after primary and retreatment procedures, and often exhibit a biofilm growth mode that increases resistance to disinfection [ 10 ]. This anatomical feature may also negatively influence treatment outcomes [ 11 ], as residual microorganisms and debris within the isthmus contribute to the failure of orthograde treatment [ 12 ], endodontic microsurgery [ 13 ], and the incomplete filling of this area by sealers [ 14 ].

Thus, in addition to the importance of irrigation, intracanal medications also play a key role in managing microbial persistence in these complex areas. Calcium hydroxide (Ca (OH)₂) remains one of the most widely used agents due to its high pH, antimicrobial properties, biocompatibility, and capacity to stimulate hard tissue repair [ 15 ]. Recent advances have introduced new calcium silicate–based intracanal medications, such as Bio-C Temp (Angelus, Londrina, PR, Brazil), launched in 2020 as an alternative to Ca (OH)₂. Indicated for cases of pulp necrosis, retreatments, persistent lesions, exudation, or sinus tracts, its composition includes glycol salicylate, titanium oxide, calcium tungstate, calcium aluminate, calcium oxide, and calcium silicate [ 16 ].

However, despite their therapeutic benefits, residual Ca (OH)₂ may act as a mechanical barrier, impairing three-dimensional filling and reducing sealer adhesion to dentin [ 17 ]. Tavella e Silva et al. (2020) confirmed that remnants of Ca (OH)₂ decrease the bond strength of epoxy- and silicate-based sealers, reinforcing the importance of their complete removal before obturation [ 18 ]. Nevertheless, although this is clinically relevant, several investigations have demonstrated that complete removal of Ca (OH)₂ is rarely achieved using only conventional irrigation and aspiration techniques [ 19 ].

As conventional syringe-and-needle irrigation is generally ineffective in removing accumulated hard-tissue debris (AHTD) caused by anatomical irregularities, several adjunctive approaches have been proposed to improve irrigant delivery to such anatomical complexities within the root canal system [ 20 ].

Passive ultrasonic irrigation (PUI) has been widely employed to enhance cleaning and disinfection of root canal systems. Several studies have demonstrated that this technique significantly improves the cleaning of complex anatomical regions, reducing remnants of pulp tissue and debris generated during instrumentation. Additionally, favorable outcomes have been reported regarding its effectiveness in removing calcium hydroxide–based pastes [ 21 ].

Another adjunctive approach is the EasyClean instrument (Easy Equipamentos Odontológicos, Belo Horizonte, MG, Brazil), size 25/0.04, which features an aircraft wing-shaped cross-section and is made of acrylonitrile butadiene styrene, providing high flexibility and promoting vigorous intracanal fluid agitation [ 20 ]. This instrument has been shown to enhance irrigant penetration into simulated lateral canals [ 22 ].

More recently, IrriFlex (Produits Dentaires SA, Vevey, Switzerland) has been introduced as a flexible polypropylene needle with a closed end and dual lateral outlets. This double-vented needle allows the generation of two obliquely directed jets and delivers a large volume of irrigant at high flow rates, with a reduced risk of apical extrusion. However, the effectiveness of this plastic needle still requires further investigation [ 23 ].

Considering the anatomical complexity of isthmuses, their impact on treatment outcomes, and the clinical importance of effective intracanal medication removal, especially in these regions, the present study aimed to evaluate and compare the effectiveness of different irrigation activation techniques, including passive ultrasonic irrigation (PUI), EasyClean, and IrriFlex, in removing two intracanal medications (UltraCal XS and Bio-C Temp) from mesial root isthmuses of mandibular molars using 3D-printed models. These techniques were selected because they represent different approaches for enhancing irrigant action within complex root canal anatomy. The null hypothesis tested was that no statistically significant differences would be observed among the irrigation techniques.

sections.heading: Sample preparation and 3D-printed replica fabrication
paragraphs: The study was approved by the local research ethics committee (CAAE 78839024.1.0000.5419). A recently extracted mandibular first molar (Fig.  1 A) obtained from an institutional tooth bank and extracted for periodontal reasons, was selected for this study. The tooth was stored in 0.1% thymol solution, washed under running water for 24 h, and its external root surface was cleaned using ultrasonic scaling (Profi II Ceramic, Dabi Atlante Ltda, Ribeirão Preto, SP, Brazil). The tooth was macroscopically examined and radiographed (Spectro 70X Electronic, Dabi Atlante, Ribeirão Preto, São Paulo) in the orthoradial and mesioradial directions, using an intraoral phosphor plate (Eagle PS, Dabi Atlante, Ribeirão Preto, São Paulo), with the aim of selecting a mesial root with moderate curvature. An orthoradial radiograph was taken, confirming that the mesial root had a curvature classified between 10° and 25° according to the Schneider method. Furthermore, this radiograph helped to ensure that the tooth met the following criteria: fully formed root, mesial roots with isthmus, no calcifications, resorptions, restorations, or fractures.
Fig. 1 Sample preparation.  A  Extracted mandibular molar.  B  The STL file of the 3D tooth model.  C  Transparent STL rendering showing the root canal anatomy

Access to the pulp chamber was performed using a spherical bur #2 (KG Sorensen, Barueri, SP, Brazil) under high speed and constant irrigation. After access, the root canal was initially irrigated with 2 mL of 2.5% sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl) using a disposable plastic syringe (Ultradent, South Jordan, UT, USA) and a NaviTip needle with a 0.30 mm diameter (Ultradent, South Jordan, UT, USA). The root canal exploration was carried out using a #15 stainless steel K-file (Dentsply Maillefer, Petrópolis, RJ, Brazil) until its tip was visible, with magnification assistance from a surgical microscope (Opto Novus, São Carlos, SP, Brazil), and coincided with the apical foramen, reaching the actual length of the tooth. From this measurement, 1.0 mm was subtracted to establish the working length (WL), wich was standardized at 20 mm for all mesial canals.

Biomechanical preparation was performed using the reciprocating movement instrumentation technique up to the Reciproc R40.06 instrument (VDW GmbH, Munich, Germany), reaching the full working length. This preparation size was selected to ensure reproducible apical foramen reproduction during the 3D-printing process and to maintain standardized canal patency among replicas. The instrument was attached to a 6:1 reduction contra-angle driven by an XSmart Plus motor (Dentsply Maillefer, Ballaigues, Switzerland). Instrumentation followed the manufacturer’s recommendations, with passive insertion and three pecking motions per advancement. After each cycle, the instrument was removed, cleaned with gauze, and the canals were irrigated with 2.5% NaOCl, aspirated, and refilled using a disposable plastic syringe with a NaviTip needle. Final irrigation was performed using 2 mL of 17% ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) (Biodinâmica, Ibiporã, PR, Brazil) for 5 min, followed by irrigation with 5 mL of 2.5% NaOCl. The canals were initially dried using a Capillary Tip suction cannula (Ultradent Products Inc., South Jordan, UT, USA), followed by #40 paper points (Dentsply Maillefer, Petrópolis, RJ, Brazil).

After the biomechanical preparation, the tooth was scanned using the SkyScan 1174 microtomograph (SkyScan 1174 v2, Bruker-microCT, Kontich, Belgium) with the following acquisition parameters: 50 kVp, 800 µA, isotropic resolution of 26.97 μm, 360° rotation around the vertical axis with a rotation step of 0.7°, one frame, and a 0.5 mm thick aluminum filter. The micro-CT images of the scanned tooth were reconstructed using NRecon v.1.6.6.0 software (Bruker-microCT) to obtain axial cross-sectional slices of its internal structure. A 3D stereolithographic (STL) model of the tooth was then generated through binarization using CTAn v.1.18.8.0+ (Bruker-microCT).

Image processing and analysis were performed using CTAn v.1.18.8.0 + software (BrukermicroCT, Kontich, Belgium), with separate binarization of enamel, dentin, and the root canal. A 3D tooth model was generated using the double time cubes algorithm in STL format (Fig.  1 B). A realistic visualization of this model was created with CTVol v.2.3.2.1 software (BrukermicroCT, Kontich, Belgium) for subsequent refinement of the isthmus morphology, following the classification proposed by Fan et al. (2010), corresponding to type I [ 9 ] (Fig.  1 C).

The STL file of the 3D tooth model was exported to Blender3D software (Blender Foundation, Amsterdam, Netherlands), for mesh cleaning of the mesial canals and isthmus (Fig.  2 A-C). The optimized 3D model was then imported into the FlashDLPrint 3D printing software (FlashForge Corporation, Zhejiang, China), and 64 3D-printed tooth replicas were produced using a FlashForge Hunter printer (FlashForge Corporation) with digital light processing (DLP) technology (Fig.  2 D).

Fig. 2 3D Artificial Teeth mesh cleaning via STL.  A  Internal view showing the isthmus of the mesial root canal system.  B  View of the mesial canals including the highlighted isthmus.  C  View of the highlighted isthmus only.  D  3D-printed artificial teeth with isthmus

sections.heading: Intracanal medication
paragraphs: A calcium silicate-based paste Bio-C Temp ®  (Angelus Indústria de Produtos Odontológicos S/A, Londrina, Brazil) and a calcium hydroxide-based paste UltraCal XS ®  (Ultradent Products, Inc., Indaiatuba, SP, Brazil) were placed into the mesial root canal system using the manufacturers’ recommended tips. All specimens were standardized 3D-printed translucent replicas with identical canal anatomy, including a Type I isthmus. The translucency of the resin allowed visual confirmation of homogeneous filling of both canals and the isthmus region in all specimens. The medications remained in the canals, including the isthmus, for 7 days. During this period, the replicas were incubated at 37 °C with 95% humidity.

sections.heading: Re-preparation of the mesial root canal system
paragraphs: After the medication period, the mesial root canal system was re-prepared using Reciproc R40.06 instrument (VDW, Munich, Germany), following the same protocol described previously.

sections.heading: Irrigation techniques
paragraphs: All canals of the mesial root canal system were irrigated with a total of 18 mL of 2.5% NaOCl using a disposable plastic syringe (Ultradent Products Inc., South Jordan, UT, USA) and a NaviTip needle (Ultradent Products Inc., South Jordan, UT, USA). A 2.5% NaOCl solution was selected because it provides an appropriate balance between antimicrobial activity and tissue-dissolving capacity while remaining widely used in experimental endodontic studies [ 24 ]. The irrigation protocol was standardized based on previous micro-CT studies evaluating irrigation efficacy and intracanal medication removal in anatomically complex root canal systems [ 20 ,  21 ]. The irrigant was activated for three 20-second cycles according to each irrigation protocol, using 2 mL of fresh NaOCl per cycle (6 mL per activation protocol), resulting in a total irrigant volume of 18 mL for each specimen.

Conventional irrigation (CI): Irrigation was performed using a disposable 5 ml plastic syringe (Ultradent Products Inc., South Jordan, UT, USA) and a NaviTip 30G needle (Ultradent Products Inc., South Jordan, UT, USA), wich was inserted using an in-and-out motion up to 1 mm short of the working length, with continuous aspiration at the canal orifice.

Passive Ultrasonic Irrigation (PUI): The E1-Irrisonic ultrasonic tip (Helse Dental Technology, Santa Rosa de Viterbo, Brazil) mounted on an ultrasonic unit (Piezon 150, Electron Medical Systems, Nyon, Switzerland) was inserted into the root canal, 2 mm short of the working length, at 10% power.
Easy Clean (EC): The Easy Clean ®  instrument attached to a contra-angle and operated at low speed in continuous rotation up to the working length.

Irriflex (IF): The IrriFlex ®  needle (Products Dentaires SA, Vevey, Switzerland), equipped with two side openings at the tip in a single plane, was used for irrigant delivery and was positioned 2 mm short of the root apex and manipulated with an up-and-down motion during irrigation.

sections.heading: Final micro-CT scanning
paragraphs: After intracanal medication removal, the 64 3D-printed tooth replicas were scanned using the SkyScan 1174 micro-CT system. Once properly positioned, the scans were performed following these acquisition parameters: 100 kVp, 100 µA, isotropic resolution of 21 μm, 180° rotation around the vertical axis with a rotation step of 0.7°, total of 4 frames, and an aluminum/copper filter with thicknesses of 0.5 mm and 0.038 mm, respectively. The selected parameters set an average scanning time of approximately 44 min. The resulting two-dimensional image projections were saved in Tagged Image File Format (TIFF).

The images from each specimen obtained via micro-CT after intracanal medication removal were registered and aligned with the images from the initial micro-CT scans when the teeth were filled with intracanal medications. This alignment was achieved using the “3D registration” tool in the DataViewer v.1.5.1.2 software (Bruker-microCT, Kontich, Belgium). By convention, the dataset of the filled tooth was set as the fixed reference, with dynamic registration applied to the post-removal dataset, aligning it with the first scan. This newly aligned dataset for each specimen after medication removal was saved to a new directory. Additionally, a new directory was created to store the “Image Difference” dataset, representing the variance between the pre- and post-removal datasets. Following specimen alignment, image processing and analysis were conducted using CTAn v.1.18.8.0+ (Bruker-microCT, Kontich, Belgium). The region of interest (ROI) was defined as the area containing intracanal medication remnants, segmented into two regions: (1) the apical region, where the “Top” was designated as the most apical slice with visible obturation, and the “Bottom” covered the next 3 mm coronally; and (2) the isthmus region, with the “Top” defined as the first slice of the isthmus region visible on the scan. All micro-CT analyses were performed by a single calibrated examiner blinded to the experimental groups. All datasets were anonymized and coded prior to analysis. Intra- and inter-examiner reliability were not formally assessed.

sections.heading: Statistical analysis
paragraphs: The normality of the data was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test. For the statistical analysis, the percentage of remaining intracanal medication volume was analyzed using a t-test. Additionally, the percentage of medication volume removed specifically in the isthmus area was calculated. These data were then subjected to a two-way ANOVA ( p  < 0.05) to assess the effects of different factors, followed by Tukey’s test for multiple comparisons among groups.

sections.heading: Quantitative assessment of isthmus area filling volume by micro-computed tomography
paragraphs: Representative images of intracanal medication removal in the isthmus area are shown in Fig.  3 . Considering the isthmus area filling, ANOVA with Tukey’s post-hoc test revealed a statistically significant difference between removal techniques in one of the groups ( p  < 0.05). The highest percentage (%) of Ultracal XS removal was observed with PUI (98.2 ± 2.28) ( p  < 0.05) compared to the other groups, with no difference among them ( p  > 0.05). For Bio-C Temp, there was no difference among protocols ( p  > 0.05). Additionally, for the PUI protocol, no difference was observed between the intracanal medications whereas, in the other protocols, the % of removal was higher for Bio-C Temp compared to Ultracal XS ( p  < 0.05). Table  1  shows the mean and standard deviation results of different intracanal medication removal techniques in the isthmus area and different medications.

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: The incomplete removal of intracanal dressings can compromise sealer adhesion to dentin and favor microleakage [ 25 ], underscoring the importance of efficient cleaning for successful root canal treatment [ 26 ]. This in vitro study investigated the performance of four irrigation methods in removing two intracanal medications from the mesial root isthmus of mandibular molars using micro–computed tomography. The null hypothesis was rejected, as significant differences were found among the groups.

Our findings showed that PUI was the most effective protocol for Ultracal XS removal, confirming previous reports [ 27 ]. Its superiority can be attributed to irrigant agitation and enhanced fluid dynamics within complex anatomies. Ultrasonic activation promotes acoustic streaming and cavitation, with microbubble collapse generating shear forces that dislodge debris from dentinal walls, thereby improving cleaning efficiency [ 28 ]. Notably, PUI removed both Ultracal XS and Bio-C Temp medication with similar effectiveness, indicating that its efficacy is not material-dependent. The E1-Irrisonic tip enhances these effects by promoting hydrodynamic agitation of the irrigant, contributing to the removal of intracanal medication and reducing its adhesion to canal walls.

EasyClean showed lower efficacy than PUI but outperformed conventional irrigation in Ultracal XS removal. No statistically significant differences were observed between techniques when removing Bio-C Temp medication ( p  > 0.05). Prior research demonstrated that EasyClean in rotary motion achieved results comparable to PUI for smear layer removal in curved canals, whereas syringe irrigation was less effective [ 29 ]. However, this differs from the present findings, in which EasyClean showed inferior performance compared to PUI, which may be related to differences in substrate characteristics, experimental design, or the type of intracanal material evaluated. Although smear layer and intracanal medication are distinct targets, both depend on irrigant agitation and apical flow.

IrriFlex, a flexible polyethylene needle with dual lateral outlets, also showed favorable results. Previous studies reported superior performance of IrriFlex compared to closed-ended needles, particularly in the apical third [ 30 ]. In our investigation, IrriFlex was more effective than conventional irrigation in coronal and middle thirds but remained less effective than PUI in apical regions for Ultracal XS removal. Conventional irrigation consistently presented the lowest performance, leaving greater residual material. A lack of active irrigant dynamics in conventional syringe irrigation may have resulted in limited irrigant distribution and interaction with dentinal walls. In contrast, the distinctive design of IrriFlex, with its two laterally directed jets targeting the canal walls, likely promotes more uniform irrigant delivery and enhanced wall contact [ 31 ], which may contribute to improved removal of intracanal medication.

Collectively, these results confirm that although EasyClean and IrriFlex enhance irrigant effectiveness, PUI remains the most efficient strategy, particularly in anatomically complex areas such as the isthmus of mandibular molars.

When comparing the tested materials, Bio-C Temp exhibited less residual material than UltraCal XS, regardless of the activation method. This difference is likely related to its chemical composition [ 32 ]. Lower concentrations of dicalcium and tricalcium silicate result in crystal formation with limited interlacing, reduced hardening, and greater ease of removal, particularly from complex regions. In agreement with previous data [ 33 ], the present results suggest that Bio-C Temp was more easily removed than UltraCal XS under the tested conditions.

To the authors’ knowledge, few studies have directly compared the removal of calcium hydroxide- and calcium silicate-based intracanal medicaments specifically within isthmus regions. Therefore, the present findings provide novel information regarding the behavior of these materials in a clinically relevant anatomical complexity.

Previous studies on intracanal medication removal have relied on natural teeth, typically requiring invasive and destructive sectioning methods for analysis. Techniques such as SEM [ 34 ], stereomicroscopy [ 35 ], micro-CT and laser scanning microscopy [ 36 ], while informative, compromise internal canal integrity and may alter medication retention. To overcome these limitations, we used standardized 3D-printed replicas, generated from a mandibular molar scanned by micro-CT, ensuring uniform anatomy and reproducibility across groups. Following prior recommendations [ 37 ], the tooth was instrumented before scanning to prevent resin accumulation in the isthmus. Additionally, the internal morphology was checked in Blender software before printing to confirm the absence of irregularities. Unlike studies restricted to printed canal segments [ 27 ], our approach reproduced the entire tooth structure, enabling specimen adaptation to a mannequin and simulation of clinical procedures under isolation conditions.

The main methodological contribution of this study is the use of full 3D-printed mandibular molar replicas derived from micro-CT data to evaluate intracanal medication removal in an isthmus-containing root canal system. Although resin replicas do not reproduce the biological properties of dentin, they provide a highly standardized model in which canal morphology, isthmus configuration, and medication volume are consistent across specimens, allowing reproducible and controlled comparison of irrigation protocols. Additionally, this study compares the removal of Ultracal XS and Bio-C Temp medicaments specifically in the isthmus region, a clinically challenging area for debridement.

Compared with natural dentin, resin-based 3D-printed materials lack tubular structure, permeability, and biological reactivity, which may influence intracanal medicament behavior. In dentin, the tubular network allows penetration of calcium hydroxide into dentinal tubules, increasing its retention within the root canal system [ 36 ]. In contrast, resin surfaces are more inert and do not reproduce these interactions, which may facilitate medicament removal. Therefore, results should be interpreted with caution when extrapolating to clinical conditions, as they reflect comparative efficacy under standardized experimental conditions rather than direct clinical performance in vivo. Another limitation of this study is the use of micro-CT as the sole evaluation method. Although this approach provides non-destructive three-dimensional quantitative analysis of medication remnants, complementary methods could provide additional information regarding surface characteristics and material behavior.

The selection of mesial root of first molars, known for their high incidence of isthmuses (54.8% in cross-sections. 3–5 mm from the apex) [ 38 ], highlights the clinical challenge posed by this anatomy. In this study, the selected root exhibited a Type I isthmus, according to the classification of Fan et al. (2010) [ 9 ], characterized by a broad and continuous connection between canals. Root canals were prepared with Reciproc R40/06. This preparation size was selected to ensure reproducible apical anatomy during the 3D-printing process and to standardize canal dimensions among replicas. Additionally, the same instrument was used during repreparation to simulate the mechanical disruption of intracanal medication before irrigation activation, avoiding an additional variable related to apical enlargement. Although the apical third was not directly evaluated, all systems achieved partial removal of Ultracal XS in the isthmus. A limitation, however, lies in the interaction between the resin used in the replicas and the tested medications. In natural dentin, Ca (OH)₂ penetrates tubules and irregularities due to dentin porosity [ 36 ], whereas resin lacks this permeability, potentially influencing retention and removal. Despite this, Bio-C Temp, which does not require moisture to set, exhibited a softer consistency after 7 days and was more easily removed upon re-instrumentation with Reciproc R40/06, regardless of the irrigation technique. This finding may explain the higher removal rates observed in this group.

Given that previous evidence indicates that 3D-printed replicas are suitable for evaluating obturation quality in simple root canal systems, with no significant influence of temperature, position, or moisture [ 39 ] a similar effect might also be expected for intracanal medications; however, further studies are needed to confirm this assumption. Overall, the use of 3D-printed models provided a standardized and reproducible platform for evaluating intracanal medication removal while preserving complex anatomical features, such as isthmuses. Additionally, these models allow for precise control over anatomical variables and enable the replication of identical specimens across experimental groups, reducing variability and improving the reliability of comparisons. This approach represents an important methodological advance, particularly considering the limited availability and inherent variability of natural tooth specimens. Additionally, the standardized irrigation protocol allowed controlled comparison among groups by minimizing variations in irrigant volume and activation parameters.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: It is concluded that, within the limitations of this in vitro study, PUI promoted greater removal of UltraCal XS from the isthmus region compared with the other irrigation protocols tested. For Bio-C Temp, no differences were observed among the irrigation techniques. Additionally, Bio-C Temp showed greater removability than UltraCal XS under the experimental conditions evaluated.
